definition: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." The unifying explanation of reward hacking, benchmark gaming, and metric-chasing product decisions.
details: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." The unifying explanation of reward hacking, benchmark gaming, and metric-chasing product decisions. The practical antidote: multiple metrics, held-out measures, and human spot checks.

explainer.lead: Goodhart's Law explains why a useful score can become misleading once people or AI systems are pushed to maximize it. It matters whenever rewards, benchmarks, or business metrics stand in for a broader goal.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a teacher gives gold stars for reading lots of pages. If you start racing through pages without understanding them, you earn stars without becoming a better reader. A number that was useful at first stops showing what you really care about.
tiers.practitioner: Use Goodhart's Law as a warning when optimizing rewards, leaderboard scores, or product KPIs. Combine several metrics, evaluate on held-out measures, and use human spot checks to catch reward hacking and other superficial wins. Watch especially for cases where the optimized number rises while actual quality stalls or falls.
tiers.paperLevel: In plain-text notation: let M be a measure used as a proxy for goal G. When M becomes an optimization target, improvements in M can cease to indicate improvements in G. The practical response is to triangulate with multiple metrics, held-out measures, and human inspection rather than trusting one optimized score.

explainer.example: A support team makes the number of closed tickets its main target. Staff start closing tickets quickly, including unresolved ones, so the closure count rises while customers still need help. The measure has stopped reliably indicating good support.

usedIn.name: AI model training
usedIn.detail: Explains reward hacking when a system maximizes its reward signal without achieving the intended behavior.

usedIn.name: Benchmark evaluation
usedIn.detail: Frames benchmark gaming, where higher scores stop reflecting broader capability.

usedIn.name: Product decision-making
usedIn.detail: Warns against chasing a single business metric while the underlying product goal is neglected.

explainer.intuition: A measure is often only a stand-in for what you actually want. Once success is defined entirely by that stand-in, optimizing it can pull behavior away from the real goal.
howItWorks: Choose a measurable proxy for a broader goal.
Turn that proxy into a reward, target, or benchmark.
People or AI systems find ways to increase the proxy.
The score improves while its connection to the real goal weakens.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides one explanation for reward hacking, benchmark gaming, and metric-chasing product decisions. Multiple metrics, held-out measures, and human spot checks make it harder for a single gamed number to hide poor outcomes.
misconceptions: It does not mean measurement is useless; it warns about treating one measure as the whole goal.
A rising metric is not proof that the underlying outcome improved.
It applies to human organizations and product decisions as well as AI systems.
